terms.gloss: Russian proverb 'work is not a wolf, it won't run off into the forest', i.e. an excuse for laziness
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering is meaningless in English; the proverb's logic (wolf runs away) must be conveyed or replaced

proposed.en: the proverb that 'work won't run away from you'
proposed.zh: 俄谚“活儿不会自己跑掉”
proposed.ja: 「仕事は狼ではない（逃げていかない）」というロシアのことわざ

terms.gloss: to lecture in a condescending, mentor-like tone
terms.why_hard: Conveys authorial irony toward Durov's didacticism; 'mentor' alone loses the mocking tone

terms.gloss: Ivan Goncharov, 19th-century Russian novelist, author of Oblomov
terms.why_hard: Needs full name and a hint that he wrote Oblomov for readers who don't know him

terms.gloss: Durov's charge that Goncharov romanticizes laziness
terms.why_hard: The ironic inversion (praising idleness) is the segment's comic core and must stay deadpan

proposed.ja: 怠惰を詩的に美化している

terms.gloss: Oblomov, the famously indolent hero of Goncharov's novel; a byword for lethargy in Russian
terms.why_hard: 'милый Обломов' implies affectionate charm; readers may know the name but not its connotations

proposed.ja: 愛すべきオブローモフ

terms.gloss: Stolz, the energetic, pragmatic German-Russian foil to Oblomov in the novel
terms.why_hard: 'механистичный Штольц' is Durov's loaded epithet; 'mechanical' must read as dismissal, not literal machinery

proposed.zh: 机器般刻板的施托尔茨

terms.gloss: 'our wondrous country' — ironic patriotic formula
terms.why_hard: The irony of 'чудный' (marvelous/absurd) must survive; 'wonderful' alone reads sincere

terms.gloss: A classmate/interlocutor of Durov, recurring named figure
terms.why_hard: Recurring character; transliteration and role must be consistent across segments

terms.gloss: A 'reasoner' — Russian literary-critical term for a character who moralizes at length
terms.why_hard: English has no exact equivalent; refers to Durov's habit of arguing everything into the ground

terms.gloss: Slang: 'runs down / trashes everyone', rails against all comers
terms.why_hard: Colloquial register; a formal rendering kills the classroom-banter tone

proposed.ja: 誰彼かまわずこき下ろす

terms.gloss: Fyodor Dostoevsky, whom Durov dismisses as 'a terrible writer'
terms.why_hard: The shock value depends on the reader recognizing Dostoevsky's canonical stature

terms.gloss: Chekhov's play The Cherry Orchard, about an aristocratic estate sold off
terms.why_hard: Chekhov unnamed in text; must be supplied; the class debate presupposes the plot

terms.gloss: Lopakhin, the merchant in The Cherry Orchard who buys the estate and cuts the orchard
terms.why_hard: 'человек дела' (man of action) is Durov's counter-reading; needs the merchant-vs-gentry frame

terms.term: влезшее сапогами в кружевную душу Раневской
terms.gloss: Children's cliché: the merchant 'stomping in his boots' into Ranevskaya's 'lacy soul' (delicate aristocratic sensibility)
terms.why_hard: Deliberately overwrought adolescent rhetoric; must sound pompous, not translated flat

proposed.en: bursting in his boots into Ranevskaya's lace-curtained soul
proposed.zh: 穿着靴子踩进拉涅夫斯卡娅蕾丝般娇柔的灵魂
proposed.ja: 長靴のままラネーフスカヤのレースのような魂に踏み込む

terms.gloss: The class nearly came to blows
terms.why_hard: Register of schoolboy scuffle; 'fight' must stay vivid and colloquial

proposed.en: the class nearly came to blows
proposed.ja: クラスはほとんど殴り合い寸前だった

terms.gloss: 'Chronic nerds' — students pathologically devoted to maths/science, the school's top achievers
terms.why_hard: 'Хронический' ironically implies addiction/illness, not just 'typical'; 'nerd' carries different weight in Russian 2000s school slang

proposed.ja: 重度のオタク（慢性ネード）

terms.gloss: author's coinage: the 'creative stratum' of educated professionals serving end consumers
terms.why_hard: 'Strata' is sociological jargon used semi-ironically; not the same as 'creative class' (a then-fashionable buzzword it nods to)

terms.gloss: rallying slogan 'If not us, who?' fed to elite-school students about the country's future
terms.why_hard: a set Russian phrase; must read as an internalised slogan, not a literal question

proposed.ja: 「僕らがやらなければ、誰がやるのか」

terms.gloss: Pavel's elder brother, mathematics prodigy, later VK co-founder and lead programmer
terms.why_hard: recurring main character; name transliteration and the 'Durov brothers' framing must stay consistent book-wide

proposed.ja: ニコライ・ドゥーロフ

terms.gloss: Mednikov, a teacher at Pavel's school who ran the maths strand and spoke to parents
terms.why_hard: only surname given; needs identification to choose transliteration and avoid implying he's a famous figure

terms.gloss: Rukshin, celebrated (and famously harsh) St Petersburg maths-circle coach, called 'the ideological inspiration of the maths circle'
terms.why_hard: 'идейный вдохновитель' is ironic Soviet officialese; Rukshin's real reputation as a hard-driving coach is the point of Mednikov's jab

terms.gloss: maths circle, the Soviet/Russian extracurricular problem-solving club run by a coach
terms.why_hard: institution unknown to en/ja readers; 'math club' undersells its elite olympiad-training role

terms.gloss: the 'Little One', School No. 1 in St Petersburg, the elite physics-maths school where Nikolai was drilled
terms.why_hard: nickname for a specific school; literal 'unit' or 'one' is meaningless; must match whatever the school is called elsewhere in the book

terms.gloss: 'Durov the elder' — here Nikolai, as the elder Durov brother, judging the competition
terms.why_hard: a reader may misread it as the father; the Russian patronymic-style epithet must render seniority among brothers, not generation

terms.gloss: nervous breakdown in a child driven too hard by unsolved problems
terms.why_hard: a standard Russian clinical-colloquial term; 'nervous collapse' vs 'breakdown' register matters in a quote

terms.gloss: enuresis (bedwetting) as a stress symptom of over-coached children
terms.why_hard: blunt medical term used deliberately in a quote; euphemising it loses Mednikov's force

terms.gloss: the panel/board of judges at the competition
terms.why_hard: echoes Soviet 'collegium' officialese; must not be rendered as 'college'

terms.gloss: exasperated reproach to the judge-panel colleague: 'Why didn't you say anything!'
terms.why_hard: colloquial ты-form among colleagues; over-polite rendering kills the humour

terms.gloss: inner emotional experiences, private turmoil or feelings
terms.why_hard: often mechanically translated as 'personal experiences' (connoting events/work history) rather than subjective emotional inner life

terms.gloss: to bare oneself psychologically and expose private vulnerabilities online
terms.why_hard: could be misread as literal physical nudity rather than emotional/informational self-exposure

terms.gloss: permission settings/access permissions to personal profile content
terms.why_hard: sounds like state security clearance ('admission') in Russian bureaucratic contexts, but refers to social media privacy settings

terms.gloss: spilled out or poured out into public space impulsively
terms.why_hard: a careless translator might miss the visceral, uncontained imagery of dumping raw emotional contents online

terms.gloss: choking back tears or shame while struggling to confess words
terms.why_hard: literal 'choking on words' can sound purely physical rather than emotionally constrained during a confession

proposed.ja: 言葉を詰まらせながら

terms.gloss: last rites / deathbed confession in Christian tradition
terms.why_hard: might be rendered as just 'the latest confession' or a routine confession rather than the ultimate deathbed rite

terms.gloss: those who dragged/pulled the physical human world into binary digital code (programmers/tech founders)
terms.why_hard: the verb 'втащить' conveys forceful, uninvited dragging, which neutral verbs like 'brought' lose

proposed.en: dragged the world into binary code
proposed.zh: 把世界拽入二进制代码
proposed.ja: 世界をバイナリコードへと引きずり込んだ

terms.gloss: the hidden, dark, unpolished underside of human nature
terms.why_hard: often translated generically as 'inside' rather than the reverse side of fabric, meaning the unseemly secret underbelly

proposed.en: the dark underside of human nature

terms.gloss: of the highest, most incontrovertible authenticity and fidelity
terms.why_hard: clunky literal phrasing ('most authentic quality') misses the biting journalistic irony about telemetry data precision

proposed.zh: 最无可争议的真实成色

terms.gloss: a shared, distributed cybernetic biological infrastructure uniting humanity
terms.why_hard: technical biological/network metaphor that sets up the 'ЦНС' recurring motif across chapters

terms.gloss: nerve endings; points of user contact, sensory input, and data collection in a network
terms.why_hard: needs to sustain the neuro-biological metaphor without lapsing into purely dry IT jargon

terms.gloss: a deliberate public statement or artistic/discursive act in contemporary semiotic and cultural parlance
terms.why_hard: translating simply as 'statement' loses the post-modern intellectual ring of an identity-defining manifesto

terms.gloss: a play on 'the wisdom of crowds' (мудрость толпы / Surowiecki), narrowed down to social-graph algorithmic consensus
terms.why_hard: misses the direct pun on James Surowiecki's 2004 book 'The Wisdom of Crowds' tailored to social networks ('friends')

terms.gloss: an exclusive expert authority to deliver definitive, all-encompassing judgments
terms.why_hard: heavy Russian journalistic syntax requires unbundling to avoid wooden academese

proposed.ja: 決定的な評価を下す独占権

terms.gloss: Central Nervous System (центральная нервная система), here used as a tech-sociological metaphor
terms.why_hard: abbreviation needs clean recognition in target languages without being confused with cryptographic or political acronyms

terms.gloss: masters/owners of the codebase (the platform founders, architects, and lead engineers)
terms.why_hard: 'masters' vs 'owners'—captures sovereign feudal power over digital reality, echoing Durov's worldview

terms.gloss: picaresque or adventure novel genre
terms.why_hard: Could be mistranslated literally as 'adventurous romance' rather than the literary genre designation.

terms.gloss: in defiance and obstinate contradiction of the system
terms.why_hard: Translating word-for-word loses the colloquial force of deliberate, contrary contrarianism.

proposed.en: out of sheer spite and against the grain of the system
proposed.zh: 偏要跟体制对着干、唱反调
proposed.ja: 体制への当てつけと反逆

terms.gloss: Lady Gaga (genitive), used here generically with 'какой-нибудь' to evoke an absurd global pop icon
terms.why_hard: The generic particle 'какой-нибудь' nuances this into 'someone like Lady Gaga', not necessarily her literally.

proposed.zh: 某个像Lady Gaga那样的名流
proposed.ja: レディー・ガガのような人物

terms.gloss: Gazprom, Russian state-controlled energy monopoly and symbol of oligarchic/state power
terms.why_hard: Needs consistent capitalization and corporate designation in target markets without unnecessary glossing.

proposed.zh: 俄罗斯天然气工业股份公司（Gazprom）

terms.gloss: an attic/garret apartment on Nevsky Prospekt, iconic bohemian habitat of St. Petersburg
terms.why_hard: May be confused with a rooftop office rather than the classic romanticized St. Petersburg garret apartment.

proposed.ja: ネフスキー大通りの屋根裏部屋

terms.gloss: to draw dogs; an allusion to Durov's famous trademark dog mascot (the dog with a tongue/hoodie, later VK and Spotty symbol)
terms.why_hard: Translators unaware of VK's unofficial mascot (Spotty the dog) will miss the prophetic autobiographical easter egg.

terms.gloss: to be continued, the classic serialization sign-off
terms.why_hard: Losing the stock theatrical/cinematic formula turns a witty closing tag into a flat statement.

terms.gloss: Yury Saprykin, prominent Russian cultural journalist, essayist, and editor
terms.why_hard: Name transliteration standard must match across the book's editorial apparatus.

proposed.ja: ユーリー・サプルィキン

terms.gloss: editorial director / managing editor in Russian publishing hierarchy
terms.why_hard: Directly calquing as 'chief editor' conflates it with 'главный редактор' (editor-in-chief).

terms.gloss: Rambler-Afisha, major Russian media holding company formed by merger in 2010
terms.why_hard: Treating Afisha and Rambler as separate entities misses that this was a unified joint corporate brand at the time.

proposed.ja: ランブラー・アフィーシャ

terms.gloss: Kazan Cathedral on Nevsky Prospekt, situated right across from Singer House (VK headquarters)
terms.why_hard: The text omits the name, relying on reader's knowledge of the St. Petersburg topography facing the Singer House.

terms.gloss: Kazan Square (Kazanskaya Ploshchad) fronting Kazan Cathedral on Nevsky
terms.why_hard: Without spatial grounding, 'the square in front of it' sounds generic rather than St. Petersburg's Kazan Square.

terms.gloss: Nevsky Prospekt, the central thoroughfare of Saint Petersburg
terms.why_hard: Translating as a nondescript 'avenue' obscures the deliberate Petersburg atmosphere anchored by Nevsky.

terms.gloss: Singer Building (House of Books) on the corner of Nevsky Prospekt and Griboyedov Canal, housing VK HQ
terms.why_hard: Failing to realize this refers to the famous Art Nouveau Singer House overlooks the central setting of the entire book.

proposed.en: mansion on the corner of the canal
proposed.ja: 運河の角に建つ歴史的邸宅

terms.gloss: A St Petersburg restaurant overlooking Kazan Cathedral, apparently the Terrassa restaurant on Kazanskaya Street.
terms.why_hard: The generic-looking name is a proper name and its official Latin-script styling may need verification.

terms.gloss: Kazan Cathedral, the major Russian Orthodox cathedral on Nevsky Prospekt in central St Petersburg.
terms.why_hard: It should not be confused with other cathedrals dedicated to the icon of Our Lady of Kazan.

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the founder of VKontakte and central subject of the biography.
terms.why_hard: His surname and full-name form must remain consistent across the book.

terms.gloss: An emphatic colloquialism meaning that the theories radically astonished him and overturned his thinking.
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering about an exploding brain sounds violent rather than conveying an intellectual revelation.

proposed.ja: 彼の思考を根底から揺さぶった

terms.gloss: Positive psychology, here loosely associated with optimistic self-improvement doctrines.
terms.why_hard: The context may use the formal discipline’s name broadly or skeptically rather than in its strict academic sense.

terms.gloss: Napoleon Hill, the American self-help author best known for Think and Grow Rich.
terms.why_hard: The Russian text gives only the inflected surname, and translating it without identification obscures the self-help reference.

terms.gloss: A colloquial phrase meaning that people fall for or are readily swayed by manipulation.
terms.why_hard: The verb ведутся is informal and implies gullibility, which neutral wording such as “respond” would lose.

proposed.ja: 人は簡単に誘導に乗せられる

terms.gloss: Marketing portrayed as a process that stupefies and programs consumers like zombies.
terms.why_hard: The deliberately ungainly, polemical wording is stronger and more mocking than ordinary “marketing influence.”

proposed.ja: マーケティングによる洗脳

terms.gloss: An arena in which manipulators, marketers, and political actors compete through intelligence and strategy.
terms.why_hard: Поле is figurative, and the phrase frames morally dubious persuasion as a legitimate competitive contest.

terms.gloss: Competition described as Durov’s supreme inviolable value or article of faith.
terms.why_hard: Святыня has religious force; reducing it to “priority” loses the author’s ironic sacralization.

proposed.zh: 杜罗夫心中至高无上的信条
proposed.ja: ドゥーロフにとって最大の信条

terms.gloss: Ninburg, a person through whom Durov encountered the ideas discussed here.
terms.why_hard: Only an inflected surname appears, so the person’s identity, preferred romanization, and role require external verification.

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the Russian social-networking service founded by Pavel Durov, now commonly branded VK.
terms.why_hard: The historical name and typography should be preserved rather than anachronistically replacing every occurrence with the later VK brand.

terms.gloss: The headquarters or central office used by Durov and the VKontakte team.
terms.why_hard: The Russian word literally suggests a command headquarters and may be a recurring quasi-military label for the company’s offices.

terms.term: известный эксперимент с обезьянами и электричеством
terms.gloss: The widely circulated “five monkeys” parable in which inherited group rules persist after the original punishment disappears.
terms.why_hard: It is often presented as a scientific experiment despite dubious or conflated origins, so the translation should report Durov’s retelling without authenticating it.

proposed.zh: 那个广为流传的“猴子与电击”实验
proposed.ja: よく知られた「サルと電気ショック」の実験

terms.gloss: The Palace of Congresses in the Moscow Kremlin, venue of Supreme Soviet sessions televised in the late Soviet era.
terms.why_hard: Often confused with the later 'Конгресс-палас'; a careless translator may render it generically as 'Congress Hall' and lose the televised-broadcast era marker.

terms.gloss: Gorbachev's 'restructuring' reform program, late-1980s catchword.
terms.why_hard: Has established standard renderings in each language; must match book-wide usage, not be paraphrased.

terms.gloss: Gorbachev's policy of 'openness'/transparency.
terms.why_hard: Fixed loanword in English/Japanese; Chinese needs a settled equivalent used consistently across the book.

terms.gloss: The Presidium, the standing leadership body of the Supreme Soviet.
terms.why_hard: Institution term, not a generic 'rostrum'; must not be rendered as 'podium'.

terms.gloss: In the late-1980s context, a newly legalized private cooperative — the first legal private businesses of the perestroika era.
terms.why_hard: A translator might render it as the neutral 'cooperative' or 'co-op', losing the specific sense of early permitted private enterprise.

proposed.ja: 協同組合（コオペラティーフ）

terms.gloss: Clicking the TV's channel button — Soviet sets had mechanical push-button tuners, not remote controls.
terms.why_hard: The period detail is lost if rendered as 'channel-surfing with a remote'.

proposed.en: clicking the channel button on the television
proposed.zh: 按着电视机的换台按钮
proposed.ja: テレビの切替ボタンをカチカチと押す

terms.gloss: 'Pseudo-values of the consumer society' — Durov's own phrasing, quoted later in the book.
terms.why_hard: It is Durov's self-quotable slogan; must match wherever the book repeats his rhetoric.

terms.gloss: 'Kept his head clean' — Durov's metaphor for refusing TV, newspapers, and received opinion.
terms.why_hard: Durov's signature rhetoric; the odd, literal phrasing is deliberate and shouldn't be normalized into 'kept an open mind'.

proposed.ja: 頭をきれいなままにしておいた

terms.gloss: 3:30 a.m. — timestamp showing Durov replied to the interview at dawn.
terms.why_hard: Russian 'половина четвертого' = half before four, i.e. 3:30; careless rendering gives 4:30.

terms.gloss: 'This passage lit up on the screen' — indicates the interview was conducted via an online chat/messenger.
terms.why_hard: 'Пассаж' means a passage of text, not a musical phrase; and the screen must signal online chat, not a TV.

proposed.en: this passage lit up on my screen
proposed.ja: この一節が画面に浮かび上がった

terms.gloss: They corresponded by text messaging for eight hours straight — the author's interview method with Durov.
terms.why_hard: Sets up the recurring scene type of online-chat interviews; must be recognizable as IM, not letters.

proposed.en: we corresponded by message for eight hours straight
proposed.zh: 我们连续发了八个小时的消息
proposed.ja: 八時間ぶっ通しでメッセージを交わした

terms.gloss: Parenthetical asides marking who was talking to the editor (the author) and who to the developers (the subject, Durov).
terms.why_hard: Unusual device; the referent of 'герой' is Durov as the book's protagonist, not a generic 'hero'.

terms.gloss: Propiska — Soviet residential registration tying access to services, including kindergarten, to one's official address.
terms.why_hard: Untranslatable institution; needs a brief in-text cue or consistent gloss, since 'registered' alone reads as trivial bureaucracy.

proposed.zh: 户口（登记住址）在某个区
proposed.ja: 住民登録（プロピスカ）がその地区にある

terms.gloss: A plate of semolina porridge — the emblematic, widely disliked staple of Soviet child care.
terms.why_hard: Manna kasha carries strong Soviet-childhood connotations; 'semolina porridge' must be kept concrete, not generalized to 'breakfast'.

terms.gloss: Trolleybus — electric bus powered by overhead wires, a fixture of late-Soviet city transport.
terms.why_hard: Distinct vehicle; must not be flattened to 'bus', which loses the period/St Petersburg texture.

terms.gloss: The stairwell entrance of a Soviet apartment block.
terms.why_hard: No exact Western equivalent; 'front door' or 'lobby' both miss the specific Soviet-block entrance.

proposed.en: the entrance of their apartment block

terms.why_hard: The deliberately odd infiltration metaphor should not be flattened into simple political sympathy.

proposed.en: infiltrated by the spirit of dissidence
proposed.ja: 反体制知識人の精神を浸透させた

terms.gloss: A sense of belonging to a morally or intellectually select minority.
terms.why_hard: It suggests elitist self-conception, not religious election or merely feeling special.

proposed.en: a sense of being among the chosen few
proposed.zh: 一种自命为少数精英的优越意识
proposed.ja: 自分たちは選ばれた少数者だという意識

terms.gloss: Pavel Valeryevich, Durov’s given name and patronymic used here in mock-adult formal address.
terms.why_hard: Dropping the patronymic erases the classmates’ conspicuously formal and somewhat playful manner.

proposed.ja: パーヴェル・ワレリエヴィチ

terms.gloss: Anna Dmitrievna Bertova’s given name and patronymic, used in formal address.
terms.why_hard: It must be connected consistently with the diminutive Anya and preserve the reciprocal formality.

proposed.ja: アンナ・ドミトリエヴナ

terms.gloss: A teacher or mentor nicknamed or surnamed Griz who coached Durov and Bertova after lessons.
terms.why_hard: The context does not establish whether this is a surname, nickname, or abbreviation, so expansion or semantic translation would be risky.

terms.gloss: To get off one’s backside and exert oneself in pursuit of great achievements.
terms.why_hard: The phrase is deliberately blunt and grandiose; either sanitizing it or translating it literally would spoil the tone.

proposed.en: get off their backside and accomplish great things
proposed.zh: 抬起屁股去成就一番大业
proposed.ja: 重い腰を上げて偉業に挑む

terms.gloss: The Renaissance ideal of a universally cultivated, accomplished person.
terms.why_hard: It denotes the Renaissance-person ideal, not simply someone who lived during the Renaissance.

terms.gloss: Colloquial shorthand for a university faculty of mathematics and mechanics, here likely at Saint Petersburg State University.
terms.why_hard: It is not merely a mathematics course; identifying the intended faculty and institution affects the rendering.

terms.gloss: A Western expatriate manager (a partner-company representative) negotiating with VK; unnamed recurring figure in this scene.
terms.why_hard: Not just 'foreigner' — Russian business slang for a Western hired executive; must stay distinct from 'иностранец' later in the paragraph.

proposed.ja: 外国人エグゼクティブ

terms.gloss: The VK 'negotiator' — actually Durov playing a role in the staged negotiation.
terms.why_hard: Sounds like a professional title; careless rendering as 'the mediator' loses that he is VK's side, and the deadpan role-play tone.

terms.gloss: VK's 'Wishes/Gifts' service letting users send paid virtual gifts to friends.
terms.why_hard: Proper name of a real VK product; must be rendered as a product name consistently across the book, not as generic 'wish list'.

terms.gloss: VK's internal virtual currency — votes (голоса) bought with real money.
terms.why_hard: 'Our currency' reads oddly; needs the understood meaning 'VK votes' without a heavy footnote.

terms.gloss: The one-click purchase button inside VK that would drive gift buyers to the partner.
terms.why_hard: Recurring image of VK's platform power; 'button' must stay concrete, not become 'feature'.

proposed.ja: ワンクリックで買えるボタン

terms.gloss: Stock phrase 'it's business, nothing personal' — the expat's mantra.
terms.why_hard: A cliché in both languages; must keep the cliché flavor rather than paraphrase.

proposed.zh: 这只是生意，无关个人恩怨
proposed.ja: ビジネスですから、個人的な話ではない

terms.gloss: 'Reinforced-concrete' — Russify 2000s business slang for an unshakeable, hard-learned conviction.
terms.why_hard: The literal construction metaphor is idiomatic Russian; a literal translation is comic, but dropping it loses the period's boardroom slang.

proposed.ja: 筋金入りの信念として

terms.term: всему есть цена, и благородные устремления существуют, чтобы набить цену
terms.gloss: The expat's cynical creed: everything has a price, and noble aspirations exist to be priced up / used to inflate the asking price.
terms.why_hard: 'Набить цену' means to jack up the price by bargaining; must not be rendered as 'fill the price' or lose the cynicism.

proposed.en: everything has a price, and noble aspirations exist so you can drive the price up
proposed.zh: 万物皆有价，崇高理想的存在只是为了抬高要价
proposed.ja: すべてには値段がつき、崇高な理念とは値段を吊り上げるためのもの

terms.gloss: 'The guys are just haggling' — the expat's dismissive read of the Russians across the table.
terms.why_hard: 'Парни' (the guys/lads) conveys the expat's condescension; must not become formal 'they'.

proposed.zh: 这帮小子不过是在讨价还价
proposed.ja: 彼らはただ値切りしているだけだ

terms.gloss: Plush toys — one gift category in the virtual-gifts catalogue.
terms.why_hard: Minor, but it anchors the absurd specificity of negotiating percentages per category; keep concrete.

terms.gloss: A programmer at the table, typing throughout — part of Durov's staged entourage.
terms.why_hard: Not 'developer' as a job description; he is a silent character in the scene, kept as such.

terms.gloss: 'The guy in the baseball cap' — i.e. Durov himself, described externally.
terms.why_hard: The book never names him here; the epithet must be preserved as the recurring identifying tag, not resolved to 'Durov'.

proposed.en: the guy in the baseball cap

terms.gloss: 'This figure's eccentricity' — деятель is a slightly ironic label for a personage/character.
terms.why_hard: Деятель is ironic-cool in Russian; 'activist' or 'figure' alone miss the sneer.

proposed.ja: この人物の風変わりなこと

terms.gloss: Free indirect thought of the expat: 'we're all decent people here' — the negotiation has broken decorum norms.
terms.why_hard: This is the expat's internal voice (несобственно-прямая речь), not the narrator's; translators often mis-attribute it.

proposed.en: we're all respectable people here, after all
proposed.zh: 我们这里可都是体面人啊
proposed.ja: ここにいるのはまともな大人のはずだ

terms.term: разный процент с разных категорий товара
terms.gloss: The core dispute: a different commission percentage per product category.
terms.why_hard: Recurring negotiation term; 'category' and 'commission' wording must be fixed now for later chapters.

proposed.en: a different percentage commission per product category
proposed.zh: 不同商品类别抽取不同比例的分成
proposed.ja: 商品カテゴリーごとに異なる手数料率

terms.gloss: Inventory turnover — the expat's business jargon justifying differentiated commission.
terms.why_hard: Business term; must read as jargon in all languages, not casual 'how fast things sell'.

terms.gloss: A gift bought with VK's virtual currency — the whole transaction model of the Gifts service.
terms.why_hard: Recurring phrase; ties into the earlier 'наша валюта' decision and must match it.

proposed.en: a gift paid for in our currency
proposed.zh: 用我们的虚拟货币购买礼物
proposed.ja: 当社の通貨でプレゼントを購入

terms.gloss: Durov's physical mannerism: lopsided, leaning forward as he strides — the recurring body-language portrait.
terms.why_hard: The skewed-gait detail recurs as Durov's signature posture in the book; must be rendered identically each time.

proposed.ja: 少し体を斜めに、前かがみで

terms.gloss: The negotiator's theatrical gestures: leaning back in his chair, spreading his hands.
terms.why_hard: Gesture verbs are easy to garble; the scene's deadpan staging depends on them being clean and repeated.

proposed.en: leaned back and spread his hands
proposed.ja: 椅子に背をもたせ、両手を広げた

terms.gloss: 'Bellowed/yelled' — the abrupt register break when Durov shouts the 20-percent ultimatum.
terms.why_hard: The sudden volume is the joke; softening it to 'said loudly' kills the scene's escalation.

terms.gloss: Black trousers — part of Durov's uniform look (with the baseball cap) throughout the book.
terms.why_hard: Recurring costume tag; keep literal and consistent as a visual identifier of Durov.

terms.gloss: The stated purpose of the Wishes service: users gifting items to friends.
terms.why_hard: 'Товары' (goods/merchandise) here means the virtual gift items; must not become 'presents' circularly.

proposed.en: to give goods to their friends as gifts

terms.gloss: The escalating commission figures (5 → 10 → 20) that structure the negotiation.
terms.why_hard: Number sequencing carries the comedy of the reversed escalation; must not be normalized or rounded.

terms.gloss: Squirming/fidgeting in his chair — the expat's discomfort, the only tell that the tactic is working.
terms.why_hard: The physical detail is the subtext; 'ерзая' must stay small and human, not become dramatic.

proposed.zh: 在椅子上不安地挪动着
proposed.ja: 椅子の上で落ち着かず体を動かしながら

terms.gloss: The mass protests that followed Russia’s disputed December 2011 parliamentary election.
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering as generic protests would obscure the specific 2011–12 Russian protest movement.

proposed.zh: 2011年12月的反政府抗议浪潮兴起
proposed.ja: 2011年12月の抗議運動が起きると

terms.gloss: Russia’s procuracy, a state body combining prosecutorial and broad supervisory powers.
terms.why_hard: It is not exactly equivalent to an English district attorney’s office or an ordinary public prosecutor.

terms.gloss: A VKontakte user-created online community or group page.
terms.why_hard: Without platform context it can be mistaken for an informal political organization rather than a social-media community.

terms.gloss: Alexei Navalny, a Russian opposition politician and anti-corruption activist.
terms.why_hard: His name needs a consistent established transliteration, and his political role is essential to the episode.

proposed.ja: アレクセイ・ナワリヌイ

terms.term: из «Фауста»: Vi veri universum vivus vici – «[Силой] истины я, живущий, покорил вселенную»
terms.gloss: A Latin maxim presented as a quotation from Faust: ‘By the power of truth, I, living, conquered the universe.’
terms.why_hard: Its attribution and Latin interpretation are disputed, while the supplied Russian translation explicitly inserts an implied ‘power.’

proposed.en: from Faust: Vi veri universum vivus vici—“By the power of truth, I, living, conquered the universe”
proposed.zh: 引自《浮士德》：Vi veri universum vivus vici——“凭借真理的力量，我以有生之身征服了宇宙”
proposed.ja: 『ファウスト』から、Vi veri universum vivus vici――「真理の力によって、生けるわれは宇宙を征服した」

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder and chief executive of VKontakte.
terms.why_hard: His surname and full name must follow one transliteration convention throughout the biography.

terms.gloss: A person given to grand, self-dramatizing gestures and elevated rhetoric.
terms.why_hard: Russian пафосный can imply grandiosity or theatrical self-importance, not merely ‘passionate’ or ‘pathetic.’

proposed.zh: 这个爱摆宏大姿态的人

terms.gloss: Entrepreneurs who became millionaires through internet businesses.
terms.why_hard: It denotes wealthy members of the Russian tech scene, not people with millions of followers or merely heavy internet users.

proposed.zh: 靠互联网创业致富的百万富翁

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the Russian social-networking service founded by Pavel Durov.
terms.why_hard: The brand appears in several shortened forms, so VKontakte, VK and translated variants must be standardized.

terms.gloss: The legal owner of copyright or other applicable media rights.
terms.why_hard: In this piracy context it means rights holders whose authorization was not sought, not simply people who were not notified.

terms.gloss: An event space in a workshop of a converted former chocolate factory, likely Moscow’s Red October complex.
terms.why_hard: The unnamed venue may be recognizable to Russian readers, but identifying it too confidently requires external confirmation.

proposed.en: a workshop in a former chocolate factory
proposed.zh: 一座由旧巧克力工厂车间改造的活动空间
proposed.ja: かつてのチョコレート工場の作業棟

terms.gloss: A Forbes ranking or awards event for Russian internet entrepreneurs.
terms.why_hard: рейтинг may refer to both the published ranking and the ceremony built around it, while сетевой here means internet-based.

proposed.ja: 『フォーブス』のインターネット起業家ランキング

terms.gloss: Entrepreneurs whose businesses operate primarily on the internet.
terms.why_hard: сетевой can mean networked, chain-based or direct-sales business, but here it specifically denotes the internet sector.

proposed.ja: インターネット起業家

terms.gloss: An award category for the best chief executive officer.
terms.why_hard: The Russian text uses the English-derived abbreviation in Cyrillic-looking capitals; each language has its own established business usage.

terms.gloss: Yandex, the Russian search and internet-services company co-founded by Arkady Volozh.
terms.why_hard: The corporate name should remain a stable brand rather than be translated descriptively as a search engine.

proposed.zh: Yandex（俄罗斯搜索与互联网公司）

terms.gloss: Arkady Volozh, co-founder and then chief executive of Yandex.
terms.why_hard: His established name form and exact relationship to Yandex require verification and consistent treatment.

proposed.ja: アルカジー・ヴォロージ

terms.gloss: Perekopsky, a philology-faculty classmate of Durov's and recurring eyewitness source in the book
terms.why_hard: Recurring named source; transliteration must stay consistent across all segments and he's introduced here as a viewpoint character

terms.gloss: short for the Oriental Faculty (of St Petersburg University)
terms.why_hard: Clipped Russian institutional slang; a literal clip has no meaning outside Russian and the full name must be supplied

terms.gloss: short for the Philology Faculty (of St Petersburg University), Durov's faculty
terms.why_hard: The book's central institution; the Russian abbreviation must be expanded, and 'Faculty of Philology' ≠ Western 'English department' style naming

terms.gloss: Alexander Kazem-Bek, first dean of the Oriental Faculty, represented by a bust in the hallway
terms.why_hard: Historical figure with a hyphenated surname whose transliteration varies (Kazem-Bek / Kazembek)

proposed.ja: アレクサンドル・カゼム=ベク

terms.gloss: Baudouin de Courtene (Jan Niecisław Baudouin de Courtenay), famous linguist, first dean of the Philology Faculty
terms.why_hard: French-Polish surname whose spelling differs per language tradition; must match each target language's standard for the linguist

proposed.ja: ボードゥアン・ド・クルトネ

terms.gloss: 'faculty of brides' — Russian student slang for philology, historically female-dominated and jokingly seen as a place to find a husband
terms.why_hard: A period joke implying gender demographics; a literal rendering reads as an official name and the joke dies

proposed.ja: '花嫁探しの学部'（文学部の俗称）

terms.term: анекдот про разницу между программистом-интровертом и программистом-экстравертом
terms.gloss: A well-known geek joke: the introvert looks at his own shoes when talking, the extrovert looks at yours
terms.why_hard: The text assumes the reader already knows the joke and only hints at its second half; the translator must supply the punchline or the sentence is meaningless

proposed.en: the old joke about introverted versus extroverted programmers (the introvert stares at his own shoes, the extrovert at yours)
proposed.zh: 那个老段子：内向的程序员看自己的鞋，外向的程序员看你的鞋
proposed.ja: 有名なジョーク——内気なプログラマーは自分の靴を見、外向きなプログラマーは相手の靴を見る

terms.gloss: 2000s student slang for a rich, pampered kid of well-off parents
terms.why_hard: False friend of English 'major'/'majór' in other languages; slang register must be preserved

proposed.ja: ボンボン（金持ちの坊ちゃん）

terms.gloss: Direct quote of Pushkin's line 'a cloud, a darkness, a flock of beautiful maidens' (from 'Bova'), used mock-heroically
terms.why_hard: An unmarked Pushkin quotation; without recognising it, the translator renders three random nouns and loses the comic archaic register

proposed.en: a 'cloud, a darkness, a flock of beauteous maidens' (Pushkin)
proposed.zh: '一群、一片、一队佳丽'（普希金诗句）
proposed.ja: '雲のごとく、闇のごとく、美しい乙女たちの群れ'（プーシキン）

terms.gloss: Durov as a 'joker' — an unreadable wildcard figure, possibly with a card-game nuance and an echo of the Joker character
terms.why_hard: Ambiguity between playing-card joker, a jester, and the comic-book Joker; each target language may need different disambiguation

proposed.en: a joker with no easily legible qualities
proposed.zh: 一张看不出底牌的百搭牌
proposed.ja: 読み取れないジョーカー

terms.gloss: diminutive 'little white shirt' — connotes a tidy, naive, well-brought-up schoolboy look
terms.why_hard: The Russian diminutive carries social coding (clean-cut provincial kid) that a plain 'white shirt' loses

terms.gloss: recurring epithet for Durov as a slouching front-row schoolboy
terms.why_hard: 'Первая парта' is the Russian classroom's front desk = teacher's-pet connotation; a literal 'first desk' or 'first row' choice must be consistent wherever the epithet recurs

proposed.en: the slouching boy from the front-row desk
proposed.zh: 坐在第一排、微微驼背的男孩
proposed.ja: 前列の席の猫背の少年

terms.gloss: Palace Bridge in St Petersburg, the low drawbridge across the Neva between Vasilievsky Island and the Palace Embankment
terms.why_hard: Standard multilingual names exist but vary (Palace/Dvortsovy); must match the book's other St Petersburg bridge mentions

terms.gloss: Nevsky Prospekt metro station on the Moyka side of Nevsky Avenue
terms.why_hard: Geographic oddity a translator may not notice: from SPbU they walked the bridge to this station; station names need consistent rendering with other mentions

terms.term: уроженец города хоккея и едкого дыма из труб
terms.gloss: Periphrasis for Cherepovets, Perekopsky's hometown, famous for its ice-hockey team (Severstal) and polluting steel mills
terms.why_hard: The town is never named; the translator must identify Cherepovets to decide whether to keep the riddle or resolve it

proposed.en: a native of the city of hockey and acrid chimney smoke
proposed.zh: 来自那座盛产冰球和呛人烟尘的城市（切列波韦茨）
proposed.ja: ホッケーと煙突の煙の街の出身（チェレポヴェツ）

terms.gloss: general-education classes, i.e. a regular non-specialised state school track (as opposed to elite/gymnasium classes)
terms.why_hard: A Russian school-streaming term with no exact Western counterpart; careless renderings like 'liberal arts classes' misstate it

terms.gloss: 'recited half of his life' — Perekopsky monologued his whole biography at Durov
terms.why_hard: Hyperbolic idiom; must stay comic rather than literal 'half a life'

proposed.zh: 把半辈子的经历都倒了出来

terms.gloss: 'a slight burning' — the shared tingle of excitement at university opportunities opening up
terms.why_hard: Unusual sensory metaphor tied to the book's later fire/energy imagery for Durov; must be rendered the same way at each recurrence

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, co-founder of VKontakte
terms.why_hard: Must stay Pavel Durov / 杜罗夫 / ドゥロフ across the book, never 'Durov' alone in zh/ja without established surname policy

terms.gloss: Ilya Perekopsky, Durov’s university partner later VK deputy
terms.why_hard: Spelling of the surname (Perekopsky vs Perekopskiy) and given-name insertion must be fixed once

terms.gloss: the Durov–Perekopsky working pair treated as a political tandem
terms.why_hard: Russian media 2000s ‘tandem’ evokes Putin–Medvedev; a bland ‘duo’ loses that

terms.gloss: the staged campus contest they ran as cover for recruiting and publicity
terms.why_hard: Not a generic ‘competition’; later chapters treat it as a named episode

terms.gloss: female philology students, jokingly declined as a class
terms.why_hard: The -инь suffix is mocking/affectionate; ‘philology girls’ vs ‘women in the arts faculty’

terms.gloss: sharp-tongued, quick with a cutting remark
terms.why_hard: Easy to flatten to ‘witty’ and lose the slightly bitchy campus tone

terms.gloss: the dean’s goodwill as a career/access motive
terms.why_hard: приязнь is warmer than ‘favor’; ‘dean’ vs faculty head vs 学部长

terms.gloss: campus ‘beauty aktiv’: the unofficial clique of pretty, socially active female students
terms.why_hard: Soviet ‘aktiv’ plus English beauty; calquing or explaining once is a book-level choice

proposed.ja: ビューティー・アクチフ

terms.gloss: did not throw jealous scenes / make jealous rows
terms.why_hard: закатывать сцены is theatrical; ‘didn’t get jealous’ underplays the performance

proposed.ja: 嫉妬の場面を演じたりはしなかった

terms.gloss: beneath their dignity
terms.why_hard: Stock phrase; over-literal ‘below their worth’ sounds odd in en/zh/ja

terms.gloss: Durov’s line that women must not interfere with ‘creative experiments’
terms.why_hard: Sounds like art-speak; it is his self-myth of coding/pranks as creativity

terms.gloss: a tightly plotted, twisty storyline of which the contest is only an episode
terms.why_hard: Film/TV metaphor; ‘convoluted plot’ vs ‘intricate campaign narrative’

terms.gloss: a planned public-relations campaign
terms.why_hard: кампания can be political or marketing; here it is proto-PR for the tandem

terms.gloss: Saint Petersburg (the city, not the university)
terms.why_hard: Book mixes Петербург / Санкт-Петербург / Питер; pick one English/Chinese/Japanese form

terms.gloss: Cherepovets, a steel town in Vologda oblast, Perekopsky’s hometown
terms.why_hard: Unknown abroad; ‘metallurgical city’ must stay attached so the provincial contrast lands

terms.gloss: epithet for Cherepovets as a steel-industry city
terms.why_hard: металлургический is steel/ferrous, not generic ‘industrial’

terms.gloss: crammed/coached intensively by private tutors for university entry
terms.why_hard: натаскать is dog-training slang for drilling; ‘tutored’ is too polite

proposed.ja: 家庭教師に詰め込まれ

terms.gloss: Sennaya Square, a historically rough, central Petersburg neighborhood
terms.why_hard: Haymarket associations; ‘Sennaya’ vs ‘Haymarket Square’ vs 干草广场

terms.gloss: a regular parental allowance / stipend sent from home
terms.why_hard: содержание also means alimony/maintenance; here it is student pocket money from parents

terms.gloss: business connections, networking rather than literary English
terms.why_hard: связи is the Soviet/post-Soviet ‘connections’ sense, not mere ‘contacts’

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the central subject of the biography.
terms.why_hard: His surname should follow the project-wide form and not be translated or inconsistently romanized.

terms.gloss: Confers credibility, standing, or an intimidating reputation on someone.
terms.why_hard: Russian авторитет may mean prestige or underworld clout, depending on the preceding context.

terms.gloss: Literally 'hit banks'; likely refers to robbing, attacking, or otherwise targeting banks.
terms.why_hard: Without the preceding context, бил may describe physical robbery, fraud, hacking, or defeating the house in gambling.

proposed.ja: かつて銀行を襲っていた

terms.gloss: A spell-like state of collective paralysis imposed by the teacher's authority.
terms.why_hard: A literal 'magical stupor' can sound supernatural rather than describing intimidated classroom silence.

proposed.ja: 魔法にかけられたように萎縮させる

terms.gloss: To probe, expose, and puncture the vaguely feared consequence.
terms.why_hard: Расковырять is deliberately coarse and physical, suggesting picking open a sore rather than merely investigating.

proposed.zh: 把那种可怕的东西戳破
proposed.ja: その恐ろしさをほじくり返して正体を暴く

terms.gloss: A blunt colloquial verb meaning 'start yelling' or 'shout at the top of my voice.'
terms.why_hard: A neutral 'speak out' would erase the provocative and disruptive force of the imagined act.

terms.gloss: Formal expulsion from school as a disciplinary punishment.
terms.why_hard: It must not be weakened to suspension, detention, or simply being sent out of class.

proposed.ja: 学校を退学処分になる

terms.gloss: Got hit with or ended up receiving unpleasant consequences.
terms.why_hard: The slang is rueful and rough; literal translations such as 'raked in' can suggest a benefit.

proposed.ja: 結局、その両方を食らった

terms.gloss: A final annual grade of 3 on the Russian five-point school scale, meaning merely satisfactory.
terms.why_hard: Rendering it as 'a three' gives foreign readers no sense that it is a low but passing grade.

proposed.en: a barely passing grade for the year
proposed.zh: 学年总评得了个三分（及格）

terms.gloss: An aphoristic idea that some people fear fear itself rather than any concrete consequence.
terms.why_hard: It may echo the well-known 'fear itself' formula and should retain its concise paradox.

proposed.ja: 恐怖そのものを恐れる

terms.gloss: To choose direct confrontation rather than trying to defuse a dispute.
terms.why_hard: A literal 'go into conflict' is unnatural and may obscure the father's advice against escalation.

terms.term: ни с того ни с сего
terms.gloss: For no apparent reason or entirely out of the blue.
terms.why_hard: The paired negative construction is idiomatic and should not be translated word for word.

terms.gloss: To behave insolently or speak rudely to teachers.
terms.why_hard: Хамить implies brazen disrespect, stronger than ordinary impoliteness but not necessarily verbal abuse.

proposed.ja: 教師に無礼な口を利く

terms.gloss: A physics teacher, referred to colloquially by the name of the subject.
terms.why_hard: It can be mistranslated as the academic subject 'physics' or as a professional physicist.

terms.gloss: She incited or persuaded the whole class to skip school and go to the cinema in protest.
terms.why_hard: Подбила carries a mischievous instigator nuance, while уйти в кино implies collective truancy, not a school outing.

terms.term: «Я знаю, ты здесь. Я знаю, что ты боишься. Боишься нас. Боишься перемен. Я не знаю будущего. Я не могу рассказать тебе, каким оно будет. Но я могу показать тебе, как начать его менять. Я покажу мир без контроля и границ, мир, где возможно все».
terms.gloss: A close adaptation of Neo's closing monologue in the 1999 film The Matrix.
terms.why_hard: It should echo the target language's familiar official film translation rather than read as an unattributed original speech.

proposed.en: “I know you're out there. I know that you're afraid. You're afraid of us. You're afraid of change. I don't know the future. I can't tell you how it will end. But I can show you how to begin changing it. I'll show you a world without control or borders, a world where anything is possible.”

terms.gloss: Hunters of outstanding stories, describing nonfiction writers who pursue real-life narratives
terms.why_hard: Recurring authorial metaphor; must maintain the hunting imagery across the book

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte and Telegram.
terms.why_hard: Name transliteration varies across target languages; must be consistent throughout the book.

terms.gloss: A small area where young people gather to socialize or party.
terms.why_hard: Colloquial diminutive with specific youth culture connotations; literal translation loses the informal tone.

terms.gloss: An organized student event or gathering (possibly a festival or conference) that the university administration opposes.
terms.why_hard: Ambiguity with internet forum; must be distinguished as a physical event.

terms.gloss: A glamorous young woman, stereotypically interested in money and status rather than ideals.
terms.why_hard: The phrase is dismissive and tied to post-Soviet glamour culture; needs a rendering that conveys the stereotype.

terms.gloss: To snag or catch a rich man, typically for marriage or financial gain.
terms.why_hard: Highly colloquial and gendered; mocking tone must be preserved.

proposed.ja: 金持ちの男を捕まえる

terms.gloss: To badmouth someone behind their back, to verbally tear someone apart.
terms.why_hard: Literal translation is nonsensical; needs an equivalent idiom in target languages.

terms.gloss: Target group or audience (here, potential supporters), used ironically from a business context.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'clientele' sounds too commercial; need to adapt to social/political context.

terms.gloss: Flow of people passing by, metaphorically borrowed from internet traffic terminology.
terms.why_hard: In Russian it's internet slang; must avoid confusion with web traffic in target languages.

terms.gloss: A young woman belonging to an alternative or countercultural subculture (e.g., punk, goth).
terms.why_hard: No exact English equivalent; needs a term that conveys subcultural affiliation without explanation.

terms.gloss: Nerd or geek, derogatory.
terms.why_hard: Common slang but needs consistent modern equivalent that conveys mild contempt.

terms.gloss: Philology faculty (abbreviation of филологический факультет).
terms.why_hard: Russian universities use abbreviated faculty names; need to either spell out or find equivalent department name in target languages.

terms.gloss: A real character, an eccentric person.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'big original' is meaningless; need idiomatic equivalent.

terms.gloss: Philologist's Day, an informal holiday celebrated by philology students and faculty.
terms.why_hard: Not widely known outside Russia; may need explanation or local equivalent.

terms.gloss: Harley-Davidson motorcycle.
terms.why_hard: Brand name must be rendered consistently and recognizably.

terms.gloss: Deus ex machina, a plot device from Greek drama; used figuratively for a dramatic entrance.
terms.why_hard: Literal translation loses the classical allusion; need to preserve reference.

proposed.ja: デウス・エクス・マキナ

terms.gloss: Pass system, requiring ID or invitations to enter university premises.
terms.why_hard: Not common in many Western universities; need to convey that access is restricted.

terms.gloss: Artificial online personas or profile-based identities described as homunculi, i.e. small manufactured humanoids rather than full people.
terms.why_hard: The alchemical echo matters; translating it as just “fake identities” or “avatars” loses the grotesque artificial-life image.

proposed.ja: ホムンクルス的アイデンティティ

terms.gloss: The film “Pirates of Silicon Valley,” used here through its opening scene involving Jobs and a director.
terms.why_hard: The title must be recognized as a film reference, not paraphrased generically; the scene also needs checking for accuracy.

proposed.ja: 『パイレーツ・オブ・シリコンバレー』

terms.gloss: Steve Jobs, invoked as the archetypal persuasive tech visionary.
terms.why_hard: The Russian short surname form should map to the standard full English name for clarity.

terms.gloss: The book’s protagonist, Durov, referred to with the capitalized narrative label “the Hero.”
terms.why_hard: If flattened to “Durov” or “he,” the author’s mock-epic narrative device disappears.

terms.gloss: A highly effective salesman of ideas, someone unusually persuasive at pitching a vision.
terms.why_hard: “Strong-acting” is a pharmacological idiom in Russian; literal translation sounds odd or medicinal in English.

proposed.zh: 极具感染力的理念推销员
proposed.ja: 強烈な「アイデアのセールスマン」

terms.gloss: The book’s narrator-author referring to himself in the third person.
terms.why_hard: Choosing “me,” “the author,” or “I” changes the narrative stance and must stay consistent across the book.

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the Russian social network founded by Pavel Durov.
terms.why_hard: Brand styling matters: transliteration, translation as “InContact,” or modern “VK” all create different period and branding effects.

terms.term: so long, and thanks for all the fish
terms.gloss: The English title/phrase from Douglas Adams’s Hitchhiker’s series, quoted in Latin script in the Russian text.
terms.why_hard: The translator must preserve that the phrase is already in English and functions as a recognizable allusion, not as ordinary prose.

proposed.en: so long, and thanks for all the fish
proposed.ja: “So long, and thanks for all the fish”

terms.gloss: The established Russian title of Douglas Adams’s novel “So Long, and Thanks for All the Fish.”
terms.why_hard: A literal fresh translation may diverge from the known Russian book title and break the footnote’s explanatory function.

proposed.en: “So Long, and Thanks for All the Fish”
proposed.ja: 『さようなら、そして魚をありがとう』

terms.gloss: Douglas Adams, British comic science-fiction writer.
terms.why_hard: Needs the standard target-language form of a famous author’s name, especially in Chinese and Japanese.

terms.gloss: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy book series, cited under its standard Russian title.
terms.why_hard: The Russian title names the series by its best-known book title; target languages should use their established franchise title.

proposed.ja: 『銀河ヒッチハイク・ガイド』

terms.gloss: Vogons, the bureaucratic alien race in Adams’s series.
terms.why_hard: Established fictional race names should follow known translations rather than improvised transliteration.

terms.gloss: A hyperspace express route, the comic bureaucratic reason Earth is destroyed in Adams’s story.
terms.why_hard: The established wording in Adams translations is preferable to a flat technical paraphrase like “hyperspace highway.”

proposed.ja: 超空間エクスプレス路線

terms.gloss: Chapter heading: Chapter 1.
terms.why_hard: Seems trivial, but chapter-title formatting must remain consistent throughout the edition.

terms.gloss: The chapter title, “Botanical Garden,” likely pointing to the St Petersburg Botanical Garden area.
terms.why_hard: It is both a literal title and a specific city geography cue; overtranslating may erase place resonance.

terms.gloss: A boy carrying a volume of Cervantes, a literary detail signaling precocious intellectual atmosphere.
terms.why_hard: “Том” should suggest a substantial volume, and Cervantes should be instantly identifiable; casual wording can trivialize the scene.

proposed.en: a boy with a volume of Cervantes
proposed.zh: 手捧一册塞万提斯的男孩
proposed.ja: セルバンテスの一冊を持った少年

terms.gloss: Miguel de Cervantes, invoked as canonical high-literary reading.
terms.why_hard: Target languages should use the standard name form; the cultural weight depends on immediate recognition.

terms.gloss: The entrance/stairwell of a Russian apartment block, opening directly to the street.
terms.why_hard: “Entrance,” “doorway,” and “apartment building” are not interchangeable; this is a recurrent Soviet/post-Soviet urban space.

proposed.en: the entrance to his apartment block
proposed.ja: 集合住宅のエントランス

terms.gloss: Empty or deserted city blocks, emphasizing bleak urban periphery rather than literally abandoned housing.
terms.why_hard: “Empty quarters” can sound archaic or administrative; the image is of windswept, lifeless street blocks.

terms.gloss: High-voltage transmission towers, part of the outskirts landscape.
terms.why_hard: “Pylons,” “power lines,” and “towers” differ visually; the Russian image is specifically the tall lattice structures.

terms.gloss: St Petersburg, with the familiar local short form “Petersburg.”
terms.why_hard: Choosing “St Petersburg,” “Saint Petersburg,” or “Petersburg” affects tone; the Russian uses the colloquial local norm.

terms.gloss: The wind blows straight into his face; “физиономия” is a colloquial, slightly ironic word for face.
terms.why_hard: A neutral “face” loses the colloquial register, while slangy English can overdo it.

proposed.en: the wind hits him right in the mug
proposed.ja: 風がまともに顔に吹きつける

terms.gloss: “The sea is nearby”: a compressed sentence summing up the district’s exposed maritime climate and mood.
terms.why_hard: The brevity is stylistically important; expanding it into a full descriptive sentence flattens the prose rhythm.

terms.gloss: The Singer House (Dom Knigi), the Art Nouveau building on Nevsky Prospekt that housed VKontakte's offices
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might render it as a generic 'Singer building' without the cultural weight of it being a St Petersburg landmark and bookstore

terms.gloss: VKontakte, Russia's dominant social network founded by Durov
terms.why_hard: Must be consistent across the whole book; some passages use the full name, others abbreviate to VK

terms.gloss: The bronze Valkyrie sculptures atop the Singer House tower, personified as silent witnesses
terms.why_hard: A translator might miss that these are actual architectural sculptures on the building, not a literary invention; needs to sound poetic yet grounded

terms.gloss: Kazan Cathedral, visible from the Singer House on Nevsky Prospekt
terms.why_hard: The text says only 'cathedral' but refers specifically to Kazan Cathedral; a translator must decide whether to specify or keep the vagueness

terms.gloss: The bridges of St Petersburg, iconic city feature especially in the context of night
terms.why_hard: Alludes to the famous drawbridges opening at night; a Russian reader immediately pictures this, others won't

terms.gloss: Plunged into night, with overtones of the White Nights ending and the city going dark
terms.why_hard: In St Petersburg context, 'plunging into night' carries extra weight given the White Nights phenomenon; a flat rendering loses this

terms.gloss: A voice recorder / dictaphone used to secretly record a negotiation
terms.why_hard: The word implies covert recording and carries a journalistic/investigative connotation; 'dictaphone' in English sounds old-fashioned

terms.gloss: Nerds, transliterated from English; used here for tech-savvy people who reshaped the world
terms.why_hard: The Russian uses a direct transliteration (нёрды) rather than a native word, signaling the concept is imported from Anglophone tech culture; the translation should reflect this borrowed, slightly ironic register

terms.gloss: Shattered/broke the worldview or picture of the world
terms.why_hard: A common Russian phrase; a literal translation ('broke the picture of the world') sounds awkward in English; needs a natural equivalent

proposed.en: shattered the way we see the world

terms.gloss: The view of prefabricated apartment blocks (khrushchyovkas/brezhnevkas) seen from a commuter train, like a construction set
terms.why_hard: Evokes the monotonous Soviet-era housing blocks that define Russian city outskirts; a translator unfamiliar with this landscape might miss the bleakness implied

proposed.zh: 高层住宅像积木一样排列
proposed.ja: 高層住宅の積み木細工

terms.gloss: The jostling/crowding at the handrail in a packed commuter train or metro
terms.why_hard: A very specific Russian commuter experience; needs to convey physical discomfort and routine

terms.gloss: Road rage at drivers cutting in from the right lane, a common Russian driving complaint
terms.why_hard: Very specific to Russian driving culture; 'cutting off from the right' has a particular meaning in Russian traffic that may not map directly

proposed.en: cursing at those merging in from the right
proposed.zh: 对右侧强行并线的司机破口大骂
proposed.ja: 右から割り込む車への罵声

terms.gloss: The metro (subway), likely St Petersburg's metro given the context
terms.why_hard: In Russian, 'метро' can refer to any city's metro but here likely means St Petersburg's; a translator should not over-specify

terms.gloss: People buried in newspapers, heads down, absorbed in reading
terms.why_hard: The verb уткнуться (to bury one's nose into) is vivid and physical; a flat translation loses the image of absorption

terms.gloss: The medium/carrier (of information), here contrasting newspaper vs. phone
terms.why_hard: A technical term for information medium; must not be confused with 'carrier' in other senses

terms.gloss: Consciousness and psyche, a paired phrase common in Russian intellectual discourse
terms.why_hard: In English 'consciousness and psyche' sounds redundant or clinical; needs a natural pairing that preserves the gravity

terms.gloss: Was frightened by an arriving train, an allusion to early cinema (Lumière brothers' train) and the shock of modernity
terms.why_hard: This is a well-known cultural reference to the Lumière brothers' 1895 film; a translator should recognize the allusion to the birth of cinema and technological shock

proposed.ja: 到着する列車に怯えた

terms.gloss: A voice in the receiver at a distance, referring to the early experience of the telephone
terms.why_hard: The phrasing is deliberately archaic to evoke the wonder of early telephony; the translation should feel slightly old-fashioned

proposed.en: a voice on the line from afar
proposed.zh: 听筒里传来远方的声音
proposed.ja: 受話器の向こうから届く声

terms.gloss: Photo-pictures, a slightly diminutive/colloquial term for photos shared on social media
terms.why_hard: The diminutive suffix -картинки gives a casual, slightly dismissive tone; a plain 'photos' loses the register

terms.gloss: Subscriber/callee, a formal telecommunications term for the person on the other end of a call
terms.why_hard: Sounds bureaucratic in Russian, evoking old telecom language; using 'the person on the other end' in English is more natural but loses the register shift

terms.gloss: Nevsky Prospekt, the main avenue of St Petersburg.
terms.why_hard: Could be rendered as just 'Nevsky'; needs explanation or consistent styling as Prospekt.

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte and later Telegram.
terms.why_hard: Must remain consistent as the subject; don't confuse with other Durovs.

terms.gloss: Alexei Rutkevich, a teacher who taught psychoanalysis; likely a real St Petersburg educator.
terms.why_hard: Transliteration and whether to explain his role/surname; need know if he is a public figure.

proposed.ja: アレクセイ・ルトケヴィチ

terms.gloss: Carl Gustav Jung, Swiss psychiatrist and psychoanalyst.
terms.why_hard: In Russian just surname; English needs full name or consistent surname only.

terms.gloss: James George Frazer, Scottish anthropologist, author of The Golden Bough.
terms.why_hard: Russian transliteration Фрэзер could be misrendered as Fraser; should be Frazer.

terms.gloss: Cro-Magnons, early modern humans of the European Upper Paleolithic.
terms.why_hard: 'Cro-Magnon' has a specific anthropologic referent; not just 'cavemen.'

terms.gloss: IQ tests, intelligence quotient tests.
terms.why_hard: Need consistent rendering of 'IQ' and test term; cultural abbreviation.

terms.gloss: Hans Eysenck, German-born British psychologist who created IQ tests; exact name is Hans Eysenck.
terms.why_hard: Transliteration from Russian could yield Aizenk, but English standard is Eysenck; Chinese/Japanese need standard.

terms.gloss: 'подвергали обструкции' means subjected to obstruction/ostracism, being deliberately blocked or protested against.
terms.why_hard: Russian idiom 'подвергнуть обструкции' isn't literal; English needs 'was ostracized' or 'faced obstruction'; not just 'obstructed'.

terms.gloss: 'black race' — an outdated, now offensive racial category Eysenck used.
terms.why_hard: Highly sensitive; must preserve period discourse without modernizing or euphemizing, but with awareness of offensive connotation.

terms.gloss: Political correctness, the avoidance of expressions/actions perceived as excluding or marginalizing groups.
terms.why_hard: Term has different connotations in Russian 1990s/2000s vs current Anglophone; need consistent translation.

proposed.ja: ポリティカル・コレクトネス

terms.gloss: Sigmund Freud, founder of psychoanalysis.
terms.why_hard: Same as Юнг; need full name/surname consistency.

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the Russian social network Durov founded.
terms.why_hard: Brand name; decide whether to use VKontakte or VK; localize or keep Cyrillic name.

terms.gloss: The bulging, feminine letter 'B' of the VK logo; refers to the Cyrillic В's rounded shape.
terms.why_hard: Visual/gendered description tied to a Cyrillic letter; translators must decide how to convey shape/femininity in Latin/CJK context without losing logo reference.

proposed.zh: 那个圆润而柔美的西里尔字母В
proposed.ja: ふくよかで女性的なキリル文字В

terms.gloss: Tahoma, a sans-serif typeface designed by Matthew Carter and used widely in early Windows.
terms.why_hard: Font name must stay as proper noun; no translation.

terms.gloss: Facebook, the US social networking site.
terms.why_hard: Brand name widely known, but may need consistent use vs localized names.

terms.gloss: Pop-up notification windows, the UI elements that appear with alerts.
terms.why_hard: Need consistent term for 'pop-up windows' vs 'toasts' or 'alerts'; not just 'pop-up windows'.

proposed.ja: ポップアップ通知ウィンドウ

terms.gloss: People who have finished their turn (literally 'those who have shot'), used for people exiting an interview or exam room
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering of 'shot' would confuse; the colloquial/military metaphor needs an equivalent that conveys casual relief after an ordeal

terms.gloss: Attractive/handsome, used here by the queue members asking about the interviewers
terms.why_hard: Could be rendered as 'nice' or 'likeable' rather than the physical-attractiveness sense intended in this flirtatious context

terms.gloss: Business card (colloquial short for визитная карточка)
terms.why_hard: A formal rendering might miss the casual register; but in context the cards are unusually styled, so the word itself should stay neutral

terms.gloss: Black cards — the distinctive business cards of Durov.com Club, deliberately styled to look exclusive
terms.why_hard: The colour and material detail is important for the visual image of exclusivity; a translator might genericize to just 'cards'

terms.gloss: Reference to Harvard student clubs (likely the Harvard Crimson or a final club), evoking exclusive elite membership cards
terms.why_hard: Russian readers of 2013 would recognize the allusion to elite Western university clubs; the translator must decide whether to keep 'Harvard' generic or specify a particular club type

proposed.ja: ハーバードの学生クラブ

terms.gloss: The organization Pavel Durov ran before VKontakte, a web-studio and social club for young people
terms.why_hard: Must be kept as a proper name; a translator might try to translate 'Club' or alter the formatting

terms.gloss: Ilya Perekopsky, vice-president of Durov.com Club and later VK's commercial director
terms.why_hard: Name must be consistently transliterated across the book; different conventions exist (Perekopsky vs. Perekopskii)

proposed.ja: イリヤ・ペレコプスキー

terms.gloss: The title printed on Perekopsky's card, deliberately echoing corporate/American style
terms.why_hard: The English on the card is intentional and must remain in English in all translations to preserve the visual effect

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte and subject of the biography
terms.why_hard: Must be consistent throughout; the card shows his name in English, reinforcing his self-branding

proposed.ja: パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ

terms.gloss: Title on Durov's card, part of the deliberately American-style self-presentation
terms.why_hard: Must remain in English on the card in all languages; a translator might localize the title and lose the point

terms.gloss: Nothing else — emphasizing the minimalist, enigmatic style of the business cards
terms.why_hard: A translator might over-explain or add context; the terseness is the point

terms.gloss: Gossiped — the queue was gossiping about the people inside
terms.why_hard: Sets the tone of the scene as social/informal; a neutral word like 'talked' would lose the implication of speculation and curiosity

terms.gloss: Could barely move their tongues — exhausted from talking so much
terms.why_hard: A literal translation would sound odd in English; needs an idiom conveying verbal exhaustion

terms.gloss: Their jaws ached from chatter — physical exhaustion from talking nonstop
terms.why_hard: The physical image is vivid; a translator might flatten it into a generic 'tired of talking'

proposed.ja: 喋りすぎて顎が痛くなるほど

terms.gloss: A school desk (парта) — the specific two-seater desk found in Russian/Soviet schools, not just any desk
terms.why_hard: A translator might use 'desk' or 'table' generically, losing the school-setting detail that grounds the scene in a classroom

terms.gloss: A short-haired light-brown-haired man — this is Ilya Perekopsky being described physically
terms.why_hard: The description must be consistent with earlier/later physical descriptions of Perekopsky; 'шатен' specifically means light brown/dark blond hair

proposed.ja: 短髪の薄茶色の髪の男

terms.gloss: Glasses with glinting frames — a physical detail of Perekopsky's appearance
terms.why_hard: Minor detail but contributes to the visual portrait; must be consistent with other descriptions of him

terms.gloss: A pale dark-haired man in black — this is Pavel Durov being described physically
terms.why_hard: This is the recurring physical image of Durov (pale, dark hair, black clothes); must be consistent across the book

proposed.en: a pale dark-haired man in black
proposed.zh: 苍白的黑发男子，一身黑衣
proposed.ja: 青白い顔の黒髪の男、黒ずくめ

terms.gloss: Hair parted in the middle — a specific detail of Durov's appearance at this time
terms.why_hard: A recurring physical detail; must be rendered consistently every time it appears

terms.gloss: Nearsighted/myopic — another physical detail of Durov
terms.why_hard: Must be consistent with other mentions of his eyesight; the hedging 'кажется' (seems) should be preserved

terms.gloss: He was the one doing most of the talking / he took the lead — from 'solo', meaning Durov dominated the conversation
terms.why_hard: A musical metaphor that a translator might render too literally or too blandly; it implies Durov was the star performer

proposed.en: He did most of the talking
proposed.ja: 主導していたのは彼だった

terms.gloss: Victim — the person entering the interview room, framed as prey walking into a trap
terms.why_hard: The predatory framing is deliberate and sets the tone for the interview as interrogation; a neutral word like 'candidate' would lose the author's ironic distance

terms.term: рассеянную, чуть неестественную, но в целом убедительную улыбку
terms.gloss: An absent, slightly unnatural but overall convincing smile — Durov's performed charisma
terms.why_hard: This is a key characterization of Durov's social performance; the three-adjective structure must be preserved in rhythm and meaning

proposed.en: an absent, slightly unnatural, yet on the whole convincing smile
proposed.zh: 一种心不在焉的、略显不自然的、但总体令人信服的微笑
proposed.ja: どこか上の空で、やや不自然だが、全体としては説得力のある微笑

terms.gloss: With the voice of a self-assured senior schoolboy — Durov was a university student but adopted the tone of a confident older schoolboy
terms.why_hard: The comparison is precise: not just 'confident' but specifically the confidence of a senior pupil, which implies a certain youthful arrogance; 'старшеклассник' must not become 'student' generically

proposed.en: in the voice of a self-assured senior schoolboy
proposed.zh: 带着一个自信的高年级学生的口吻
proposed.ja: 自信満々な上級生の声で

terms.gloss: A classmate or peer of Durov who championed mathematics.
terms.why_hard: Surname only; a careless translator might invent a first name or misattribute gender.

terms.gloss: A classmate or peer who championed linguistics.
terms.why_hard: Surname only; spelling must be fixed once (Paperno) to stay consistent.

terms.gloss: A classmate or peer who dreamed of shipbuilding.
terms.why_hard: Could be misread as 'Russian' adjective; it's a surname here.

terms.gloss: Colloquial: dreamed up grandiose plans, fantasized ambitiously.
terms.why_hard: Not standard Russian; flattening to 'thought' loses the mocking tone toward big talkers.

terms.gloss: Colloquial/vulgar: mocked, made fun of someone.
terms.why_hard: Register matters; too polite loses the sneering student tone, too crude distorts.

terms.gloss: Female practitioner of aikido.
terms.why_hard: Gendered Russian form; English must decide whether to mark gender.

terms.gloss: A female classmate who practiced aikido, object of teasing.
terms.why_hard: Genitive feminine surname; transliteration must be fixed (Bertova).

terms.gloss: Durov's one-word answer about his future: a totem.
terms.why_hard: Key book-defining metaphor; must not be literalized as an object or softened.

terms.gloss: Durov's stated ambition: to become an internet totem, an icon revered by users.
terms.why_hard: Central motif; inconsistent rendering breaks the book's arc.

proposed.ja: インターネットのトーテム

terms.gloss: 'Captain's Bridge', a nickname for a spot on the staircase in the philology building.
terms.why_hard: In-house nickname; translating literally without quotes confuses readers.

terms.gloss: 'The School', nickname for the philology faculty building/corridor.
terms.why_hard: Generic word used as a proper nickname; needs quotes or capitalization to avoid banality.

terms.gloss: International Student Identity Card, advertised on a bulletin board.
terms.why_hard: Keep acronym; explaining too much breaks the period texture.

terms.gloss: Finno-Ugric dialects, a seminar topic at the philology faculty.
terms.why_hard: Academic term must stay exact, not genericized to 'linguistics'.

proposed.ja: フィン・ウゴル諸語の方言

terms.term: Двоечников, не сдавших хвосты до пятницы, повесят в деканате
terms.gloss: Joking notice: 'Students with bad grades who don't clear their arrears by Friday will be hanged in the dean's office.'
terms.why_hard: Slang 'хвосты' (exam arrears) and mock-execution humor; literal 'tails' is nonsense.

proposed.en: slackers who don't clear their failed exams by Friday will be strung up in the dean's office
proposed.zh: 挂科未清者周五前将被“吊死”在系办
proposed.ja: 金曜までに追試を済ませない落単者は事務室で吊るされる

terms.gloss: Student slang: accumulated failed exams or unfinished coursework, arrears.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'tails' is meaningless; needs student-jargon equivalent.

terms.gloss: Dean's office of the faculty.
terms.why_hard: Russian academic institution; 'faculty office' vs 'dean's office' must be chosen once.

terms.gloss: 'Eurasia', nickname for lecture hall No. 215.
terms.why_hard: Room nickname; must not be mistaken for the continent or a political term.

terms.gloss: Classroom/lecture hall number 215.
terms.why_hard: Russian 'аудитория' = classroom, not auditorium; false friend.

terms.gloss: Colloquial abbreviation for the philology faculty.
terms.why_hard: Clipped slang form; spelling out loses campus texture.

terms.gloss: Colloquial abbreviation for the faculty of Eastern/Oriental studies.
terms.why_hard: Obscure Soviet-style abbreviation; careless rendering as 'eastern faculty' loses specificity.

terms.gloss: Colloquial: lanky, very tall girls.
terms.why_hard: Gendered slang; neutral 'tall' loses the teasing physicality.

terms.gloss: Student aesthetics and design contest named 'Olymp', effectively a beauty pageant.
terms.why_hard: Euphemistic official name; must hint at beauty-pageant reality without overexplaining.

proposed.zh: “奥林匹斯”学生美学与设计大赛
proposed.ja: 学生美学デザインコンテスト「オリンプ」
